title: Americans use different information routes for different public and consumer topics
source_unit: Pew Research Center survey of U.S. adults, March 6-9, 2026

denominator.unit: U.S. adults; topic-specific valid percentage bases

healthcare_news_government_social_family.unit: percent naming news media / government / social media / friends-family as main source

elections_news_government_social_school.unit: percent naming news media / government / social media / school as main source

immigration_news_government_social_famil.unit: percent naming news media / government / social media / friends-family as main source

economy_news_government_social_family.unit: percent naming news media / government / social media / friends-family as main source

social_security_news_government_social_f.unit: percent naming news media / government / social media / friends-family as main source

foreign_policy_news_government_social_fa.unit: percent naming news media / government / social media / friends-family as main source

technology_media_regulation_news_governm.unit: percent naming news media / government / social media as main source

observations.method: Pew Research Center topic-specific survey question asking U.S. adults for their main information source among news media, government sources, social media, friends/family/acquaintances, school/formal education, other, or no information.
observations.uncertainty: Cross-sectional self-reported source choice does not measure accuracy, trust quality, exposure frequency, algorithmic ranking, persuasion, or later behavior. Topic bases and nonresponse differ.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults; topic-specific distributions across information-source categories.
observations.counterinterpretation: Naming a source as primary does not mean exclusive use, trust, agreement, or reliance for a decision; source choice may reflect topic complexity, personal experience, or availability.

boundary: This record establishes topic-specific information-source distributions. It does not establish source accuracy, trust, political persuasion, consumer action, policy understanding, platform causality, or durable institutional legitimacy.
